title: Narakasura Vadham
body:
Narakasura Vadham

Narakasura was the son of Bhoomi Devi, a mighty asura who, allied with Banasura, became a force to be reckoned with. To display his dominance he conquered vast territories and struck fear across the three worlds. He kidnapped sixteen thousand and one maidens from various kingdoms, intending to offer them in sacrifice to Kamakhya Devi, and he stormed into Amaravati, the heavenly capital of Indra, plundering its treasures — the divine elephants of Indra, the umbrella of Varuna, and the sacred earrings of Mother Aditi. Humiliated and powerless, Indra mounted his elephant Airavata and fled to Dwaraka, where he narrated the asura's atrocities and begged Krishna to recover Mother Aditi's earrings and restore peace to the heavens.
Krishna, accompanied by Satyabhama, mounted Garuda and set out for Pragjyothisham, the heavily fortified kingdom of Narakasura in the land of modern-day Assam. Satyabhama, an incarnation of Bhoomi Devi and thus Narakasura's mother in a previous birth, had a significant part to play, for she was deeply enraged by his cruelty and vowed to aid Krishna in ending it. Aware of Krishna's power, Naraka had ringed his kingdom with elaborate traps, but Krishna dismantled them one by one. The first was an enchanted boulder set to crush any who approached, which Krishna shattered with a single swing of His mace. The second was a swirling pit of fire, which His Sudarshana Chakra absorbed and extinguished in an instant. The third was the demon Mura, Naraka's commander-inchief, a warrior of immense strength who wielded celestial weapons; Krishna countered his every assault and struck him down, and when Mura's seven sons charged in vengeance, they too fell before the Lord.
At last Narakasura himself came onto the field, wielding weapons granted by the Devas, and the earth trembled as the two clashed. Naraka loosed storms of arrows and mystical attacks, and at one point wounded Krishna — an act that so enraged Satyabhama that she took up arms and struck him with all her might, weakening him. Realizing his end was near, Naraka unleashed his most powerful weapon, the Shakti Astra, but Krishna shattered it in mid-air, and with Satyabhama beside Him released the divine arrow that struck the asura down and ended his reign of terror.
As he lay dying, Narakasura, humbled and repentant, made a final request: that on one day each year the sacred waters of Ganga reach all souls, allowing them to atone for their sins, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly. Krishna, ever compassionate, granted the wish, declaring that the day would henceforth be celebrated as Naraka Chaturdashi, a festival of light and purification marking the victory of dharma over adharma. He then freed the sixteen thousand and one captive maidens; to protect their honor and ensure they would not be cast out by society, He accepted them as His queens, granting them dignity and security. He placed Naraka's son Bhagadatta upon the throne of Pragjyothisham, and recovered the stolen treasures — Indra's elephants, Varuna's umbrella, and Mother Aditi's earrings — restoring peace to the heavens and the earth.
